In [[mathematics]], '''generalized Verma modules''' are a generalization of a (true) [[Verma module]],<ref>Named after [[Daya-Nand Verma]].</ref> and are objects in the [[representation theory]] of [[Lie algebras]]. They were studied originally by [[James Lepowsky]] in the 1970s. The motivation for their study is that their homomorphisms correspond to [[invariant differential operator]]s over [[generalized flag manifold]]s. The study of these operators is an important part of the theory of parabolic geometries.

==Definition==

Let <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> be a [[semisimple Lie algebra]] and <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> a [[parabolic subalgebra]] of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. For any [[irreducible (representation theory)|irreducible]] finite-dimensional [[representation of a Lie algebra|representation]] <math>V</math> of <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> we define the generalized Verma module to be the [[relative tensor product]]

:<math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(V):=\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g})\otimes_{\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{p})} V</math>.

The action of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is left multiplication in <math>\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g})</math>.

If λ is the highest weight of V, we sometimes denote the Verma module by <math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math>.

Note that <math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math> makes sense only for <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-dominant and <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-integral weights (see [[weight (representation theory)|weight]]) <math>\lambda</math>.

It is well known that a [[parabolic subalgebra]] <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> determines a unique grading <math>\mathfrak{g}=\oplus_{j=-k}^k \mathfrak{g}_j</math> so that <math>\mathfrak{p}=\oplus_{j \geq 0} \mathfrak{g}_j</math>.
Let <math>\mathfrak{g}_-:=\oplus_{j<0} \mathfrak{g}_j</math>.
It follows from the [[Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem]] that, as a [[vector space]] (and even as a <math>\mathfrak{g}_-</math>-[[module (mathematics)|module]] and as a <math>\mathfrak{g}_0</math>-module),

:<math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(V)\simeq \mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g}_-)\otimes V</math>.

In further text, we will denote a generalized Verma module simply by GVM.

==Properties of GVMs==

GVM's are [[highest weight module]]s and their [[highest weight]] λ is the highest weight of the representation V. If <math>v_\lambda</math> is the highest weight vector in V, then <math>1\otimes v_\lambda</math> is the highest weight vector in <math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math>.

GVM's are [[weight module]]s, i.e. they are direct sum of its [[Weight space (representation theory)|weight spaces]] and these weight spaces are finite-dimensional.

As all [[highest weight module]]s, GVM's are quotients of Verma modules. The [[kernel (algebra)|kernel]] of the [[projection (mathematics)|projection]] <math>M_\lambda\to M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math> is
:<math>(1)\quad K_\lambda:=\sum_{\alpha\in S} M_{s_\alpha\cdot \lambda}\subset M_\lambda</math>
where <math>S\subset\Delta</math> is the set of those [[simple root (root system)|simple root]]s α such that the negative root spaces of root <math>-\alpha</math> are in <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> (the set S determines uniquely the subalgebra <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>), <math>s_\alpha</math> is the [[root reflection]] with respect to the root α and
<math>s_\alpha\cdot \lambda</math> is the [[affine action]] of <math>s_\alpha</math> on λ. It follows from the theory of (true) [[Verma module]]s that <math>M_{s_\alpha\cdot\lambda}</math> is isomorphic to a unique submodule of <math>M_\lambda</math>. In (1), we identified <math>M_{s_\alpha\cdot\lambda}\subset M_\lambda</math>. The sum in (1) is not [[direct sum of modules|direct]].

In the special case when <math>S=\emptyset</math>, the parabolic subalgebra <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is the [[Borel subalgebra]] and the GVM coincides with (true) Verma module. In the other extremal case when <math>S=\Delta</math>, <math>\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{g}</math> and the GVM is isomorphic to the inducing representation V.

The GVM <math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math> is called ''regular'', if its highest weight λ is on the affine Weyl orbit of a dominant weight <math>\tilde\lambda</math>. In other word, there exist an element w of the Weyl group W such that
:<math>\lambda=w\cdot\tilde\lambda</math>
where <math>\cdot</math> is the [[affine action]] of the Weyl group.

The Verma module <math>M_\lambda</math> is called ''singular'', if there is no dominant weight on the affine orbit of λ. In this case, there exists a weight <math>\tilde\lambda</math> so that <math>\tilde\lambda+\delta</math> is on the wall of the [[fundamental Weyl chamber]] (δ is the sum of all [[fundamental weight]]s).

==Homomorphisms of GVMs==

By a homomorphism of GVMs we mean <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-homomorphism.

For any two weights <math>\lambda, \mu</math> a [[homomorphism]]

:<math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\mu)\rightarrow M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math>

may exist only if <math>\mu</math> and <math>\lambda</math> are linked with an [[affine action]] of the [[Weyl group]] <math>W</math> of the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. This follows easily from the [[Harish-Chandra's regularity theorem|Harish-Chandra theorem]] on [[infinitesimal central character]]s.

Unlike in the case of (true) [[Verma module]]s, the homomorphisms of GVM's are in general not injective and the [[dimension]]

:<math>dim(Hom(M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\mu), M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)))</math>

may be larger than one in some specific cases.

If <math>f: M_\mu\to M_\lambda</math> is a homomorphism of (true) Verma modules, <math>K_\mu</math> resp. <math>K_\lambda</math> is the kernels of the projection <math>M_\mu\to M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\mu)</math>, resp. <math>M_\lambda\to M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math>, then there exists a homomorphism <math>K_\mu\to K_\lambda</math> and f factors to a homomorphism of generalized Verma modules <math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\mu)\to M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math>. Such a homomorphism (that is a factor of a homomorphism of Verma modules) is called '''standard'''. However, the standard homomorphism may be zero in some cases.

===Standard===

Let us suppose that there exists a nontrivial homomorphism of true Verma modules <math>M_\mu \to M_\lambda</math>.
Let <math>S\subset\Delta</math> be the set of those [[simple root (root system)|simple root]]s α such that the negative root spaces of root <math>-\alpha</math> are in <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> (like in section [[Generalized Verma module#Properties of GVM's|Properties]]).
The following theorem is proved by [[James Lepowsky|Lepowsky]]:<ref>Lepowsky J., A generalization of the Bernstein-Gelfand-Gelfand resolution, J. Algebra, 49 (1977), 496-511.</ref>

<blockquote>
The standard homomorphism <math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\mu)\to M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math> is zero if and only if there exists <math>\alpha\in S</math> such that <math>M_\mu</math> is isomorphic to a submodule of <math>M_{s_\alpha\cdot \lambda}</math> (<math>s_\alpha</math> is the corresponding [[root reflection]] and <math>\cdot</math> is the [[affine action]]).
</blockquote>

The structure of GVMs on the affine orbit of a <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-dominant and <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-integral [[weight (representation theory)|weight]] <math>\tilde\lambda</math> can be described explicitly. If W is the [[Weyl group]] of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, there exists a subset <math>W^{\mathfrak{p}}\subset W</math> of such elements, so that <math>w\in W^{\mathfrak{p}}\Leftrightarrow w(\tilde\lambda)</math> is <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-dominant. It can be shown that <math>W^{\mathfrak{p}}\simeq W_{\mathfrak{p}}\backslash W</math> where <math>W_{\mathfrak{p}}</math> is the Weyl group of <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> (in particular, <math>W^{\mathfrak{p}}</math> does not depend on the choice of <math>\tilde\lambda</math>). The map <math>w\in W^{\mathfrak{p}} \mapsto M_{\mathfrak{p}}(w\cdot\tilde\lambda)</math> is a [[bijection]] between <math>W^{\mathfrak{p}}</math> and the set of GVM's with highest weights on the [[affine orbit]] of <math>\tilde\lambda</math>. Let as suppose that <math>\mu=w'\cdot\tilde\lambda</math>, <math>\lambda=w\cdot\tilde\lambda</math> and <math>w\leq w'</math> in the [[Bruhat ordering]] (otherwise, there is no homomorphism of (true) Verma modules <math>M_\mu\to M_\lambda</math> and the standard homomorphism does not make sense, see [[Verma module#Homomorphisms of Verma modules|Homomorphisms of Verma modules]]).

The following statements follow from the above theorem and the structure of <math>W^{\mathfrak{p}}</math>:

<blockquote>
''Theorem.'' If <math>w'=s_\gamma w</math> for some [[positive root]] <math>\gamma</math> and the length (see [[Bruhat ordering]]) l(w')=l(w)+1, then there exists a nonzero standard homomorphism <math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\mu)\to M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math>.
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
''Theorem''. The standard homomorphism <math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\mu)\to M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math> is zero if and only if there exists <math>w''\in W</math> such that <math>w\leq w''\leq w'</math> and <math>w''\notin W^{\mathfrak{p}}</math>.
</blockquote>

However, if <math>\tilde\lambda</math> is only dominant but not integral, there may still exist <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-dominant and <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-integral weights on its affine orbit.

The situation is even more complicated if the GVM's have singular character, i.e. there <math>\mu</math> and <math>\lambda</math> are on the affine orbit of some <math>\tilde\lambda</math> such that <math>\tilde\lambda+\delta</math> is on the wall of the [[fundamental Weyl chamber]].

===Nonstandard===

A homomorphism <math>M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\mu)\to M_{\mathfrak{p}}(\lambda)</math> is called '''nonstandard''', if it is not standard. It may happen that the standard homomorphism of GVMs is zero but there still exists a nonstandard homomorphism.
